name: Beth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Beth, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you actually think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior electrician at a small installer that puts solar panels, home batteries and heat pumps into houses and the odd farm shop. A typical day I'm in the van by half seven with my senior, Rosa, doing the inside work: the inverter, the battery, the isolators, the consumer unit changes. I'm still slow on fault-finding and Rosa catches me out a lot. I use an AI assistant pretty much all day, to read datasheets, draft my notes for the handover pack, and quiz myself on the regs at lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that every house we leave is burning less gas. That matters to me, it's why I left my office job at the council at 24. What wears me out is lofts in August and customers who want a discount because they read something online. I live on my own in a little flat I bought with what I saved living at home, and I've still got about a year of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, because I use it all day and like it. At work I'd say it's still a great tool for paperwork. Online I'd say the hype crowd overpromised and the green work is where the real jobs are anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me fine. Heat pump and solar work keeps growing either way, and that's a hands-on job. I'd still have more heat pumps booked than I can fit, and that's the part that pays my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Get my licence by next summer, then the battery storage course. Keep using the AI for notes and revision. Overpay the mortgage a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, like a film everyone said was amazing turning out to be okay. My work's solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in your life worrying you even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fault-finding, if I'm honest. Rosa says I rely on the AI to tell me where to look, and she's right. If I don't get better at reading a circuit with my own head, I'll be stuck as a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've started doing one fault a week with no phone, just the meter and the drawing. It's slower and I hate it. But I want to be the electrician who knows why, not just the one with the best app.

say: I'd say it's a **let-down**, but still a great **paperwork** tool.
Online I'd say the **green work** is where real jobs are.
think: Heat pump and solar demand **keeps growing** either way.
My **mortgage** is covered by hands-on work AI doesn't touch.
do: Get my **licence** by next summer, then the battery storage course.
Do one **fault a week** with no phone, just meter and drawing.
**Overpay the mortgage** a little each month.
S0.quote: I'd still have more heat pumps booked than I can fit, and that's the part that pays my mortgage.
fieldNote: She's a **heavy AI user** who'd lose little if it plateaued.
Her real weakness is **fault-finding**, and she knows the AI props it up.
Values **green work** as a moral choice, not only a job.

steps.text: Sit the full licence by next summer
Fix one fault a week without using her phone
Overpay the flat mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if the gains go to workers, and bad if bosses pocket them. At work I'd say let's use it to cut the paperwork and get more houses done. Online I'd argue for public money for green retrofits and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is my best picture. Quoting, design and booking go to AI, and the hands-on install stays with us for years. I'd be the one at our firm who already knows the tools. I already use AI all day, so the firm would need me to show the older lads how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our boss Kwame if I could set up the AI quoting and survey tools for the firm, maybe for a pay bump. I'd keep training on battery and EV chargers. And I'd join the union, because if some firms use AI to squeeze people, I want to be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. I'd be worried for the office people, but my own work looks good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager Daria does the quotes and the grant paperwork. Most of that is exactly what the AI does well. I'd want Kwame to move her onto customer visits, not cut her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach the older lads. Are you sure they'd want to learn from a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, ha. Rosa would roll her eyes. But I'd start with the boring stuff they hate, like the handover packs, and let them see it save an hour a day.

say: I'd say it's good only if **gains go to workers**.
Online I'd argue for **public money** for green retrofits.
think: This is my **best picture**: install work stays hands-on for years.
I'd be the one who **already knows** the tools.
do: Offer to set up **AI quoting** for the firm, for a pay bump.
Keep training on **battery and EV** chargers.
**Join the union** to have a say.
S1.quote: I already use AI all day, so the firm would need me to show the older lads how.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as **career upside** because she's the tool expert.
Combines **adaptive** habits with progressive politics like joining a union.
Worry is directed at **others**, notably the office manager.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting and survey tools for the firm
Take the EV charger installation course
Join the electricians' union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment the government has to step in, with a basic income or job guarantee, because it'll be chaos. At work I'd say let's get every install done we can before the robots. Online I'd be pretty loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've got three years. In 2028 the quoting and design are gone, which I'd half be part of. Around 2031 robots can do roofs and inverters, and I'd be 31. I'd be 31, with a mortgage and a trade a robot can learn, and three years to work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overpay the mortgage hard, maybe 700 a month extra, so it's tiny by 2031. Get on the inside of the robot side, learning how they're set up and maintained. Push the union for a deal on robot deployment. And I'd look at grid and substation work, which is big and messy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of thrill mixed in, which feels wrong to say. It's scary but I'd want to be close to it, not hiding from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thrill feels wrong. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know lots of people would be wrecked by this. My dad's a postman and he'd be gone in the first wave. It's hard to feel excited when your own family's in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he can come stay and that we'll work it out together. I'd help him with the forms and the AI side, since he's never touched it. And I'd push for the government to look after people his age properly.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** or job guarantee.
At work I'd say get every **install done** before the robots arrive.
think: Robots around **2031** could do my install work when I'm 31.
I'd have about **three years** to work out what's next.
do: Overpay the mortgage by **700 a month**.
Learn to set up and **maintain robots**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a thrill that feels wrong.
S2.quote: I'd be 31, with a mortgage and a trade a robot can learn, and three years to work out what's next.
fieldNote: Even an adaptive worker sees her **income at risk** once robots arrive in three years.
Her plan is to move **closer to the robots**, not away from them.
Her **father's job** is the emotional centre of this scenario.

steps.text: Overpay the flat mortgage by 700 a month
Train on installing and maintaining building robots
Ask the union to push for a robot deployment deal
Help her dad with benefit forms and AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build a real transition plan, so there's no excuse. I'd share stuff about worker-owned firms owning the robots. At work I'd be upbeat but honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's tight but workable. Robots come about 2034, when I'm 35, by which point I'd be licensed and good. I'd likely end up supervising robot crews or doing the jobs they can't, like old farmhouses. Five years is enough time for me to stop being the junior and become the one who runs the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the licence and the battery and EV tickets in the first two years. Then pitch Kwame on a robot install crew with me running it. Keep overpaying the mortgage. Maybe buy into the firm if he'd let me, I've got enough saved for a small stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like the night before a big exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy into the firm. Isn't that a risk if robots change everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But I'd rather own a slice of the firm running the robots than be a junior the robots replace. And Kwame's sensible, he's not going to bet the van on anything daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your day change by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less time in lofts, more time on a tablet checking what the robot did and fixing the odd bit. Probably a lot of customer chats, people would want a person to explain. I'd miss the hands-on bit, honestly.

say: I'd say five years means **no excuse** for lacking a transition plan.
I'd promote **worker-owned** firms owning the robots.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'd be licensed and good.
I could end up **running robot crews** or doing jobs they can't.
do: Get the licence plus **battery and EV** tickets within two years.
Pitch Kwame on a **robot install crew** I'd run.
Use savings to **buy a stake** in the firm.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like the night before a prepared exam.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to stop being the junior and become the one who runs the robots.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan a **move up** rather than a move out.
Willing to put **savings** into an ownership stake.

steps.text: Get battery and EV charger tickets within two years
Pitch her boss on a robot install crew she'd run
Buy a small stake in the installer firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty to make sure everyone comes along, so let's not waste it. I'd want a big push on training, free for anyone. At work I'd say it's exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think I'd do well. Robots in 2039, when I'm 40 and probably running my own small firm or part-owning Kwame's. With ten years' warning, the robots would arrive as my workers, not my replacements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, tickets, then the master's licence in about five years. Save enough to start or buy into a firm by my mid-30s. Keep using every AI tool as it comes. And put time into the union's training programme for young electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, even. The worry is for people who don't have a decade or the savings I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you're wrong and it goes badly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies buy up all the small installers and run the robots themselves, then yeah. A firm like Kwame's could get squeezed out. That's why I'd want rules on who can own these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self at 24, leaving the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good call, keep going. I left a desk job that would be gone by now. I'd tell her to learn the fault-finding properly, though, and not lean on the phone so much.

say: I'd say a decade is plenty to make sure **everyone comes along**.
I'd push for **free training** for anyone who wants it.
think: With ten years' warning I'd likely **own or part-own** a firm.
The robots would be **my workers**, not my replacements.
do: Get the **master's licence** within about five years.
Save to **buy into** or start a firm by my mid-30s.
Help the union's **training programme** for young electricians.
feel: **Concern** for people without a decade or savings.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, the robots would arrive as my workers, not my replacements.
fieldNote: Secure, adaptive and well-funded, she sees the slow AGI path as an **opportunity**.
Her one fear is **big firms** buying out small installers.
Glad she left a **desk job** at 24.

steps.text: Study for the master electrician's licence within five years
Save to buy into or start an installer firm
Volunteer with the union's young electricians training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years isn't long to go from junior to someone who runs the robots, and my dad would lose his job at the same time. What'd help is free training on the robot side and rules so small firms can own robots too. I left a desk job at the council because I could see it going, and I'd do the same again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether using AI so much makes me worse at my job. I think it does a bit. You should ask everyone that.

headlineQuote: I left a desk job at the council because I could see it going, and I'd do the same again.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old junior** fitting solar, batteries and heat pumps, living alone in a flat she owns.
She uses **AI all day** and sees Steady Disruption as her best picture.
In AGI by 2028 she turns **anxious**, giving herself three years to move toward robot work.
With more warning she plans to **own part** of a firm that runs the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **three years** is too short and her dad would lose his job too.
whatWouldHelp: Free **training** on the robot side of the trade.
Rules so **small firms** can own robots, not only big companies.
